courses.subject: Tefillah
courses.title: Shema: verse, recitation, attention
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on how a Torah declaration becomes a recurring practice of address, memory, and attention.

units.hebrew: שמע ישראל ה׳ אלהינו ה׳ אחד
units.translation: Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.
units.prompt: Before later interpretations, what is the verse doing in its own voice?
choices: Directly addressing Israel with an affirmation about God.
Giving a legal measurement.
Answering a Talmudic objection.
units.explanation: Start with addressee, claim, and literary setting.

units.hebrew: ודברת בם בשבתך בביתך ובלכתך בדרך
units.translation: Speak of them when you sit in your house and when you walk on the way.
units.prompt: What connection does this verse make between teaching and ordinary life?
choices: It confines Torah speech to one place.
It gives a rhythm of speaking and remembering across daily settings.
It removes the need to read the earlier verse.
units.explanation: The verse frames Torah language as recurring through a life, not detached from it.

units.translation: From when do we recite Shema in the evening?
units.prompt: What has changed when the Mishnah takes up Shema?
choices: The Torah verse disappears.
The text becomes only a historical memory.
A familiar Torah command is now treated as a practice with a time boundary.
units.explanation: The Mishnah receives the verse through a concrete question of communal practice.

units.hebrew: שמע ישראל ה׳ אלהינו ה׳ אחד
units.translation: Hear, Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.
units.prompt: What does it mean to return to the same line in prayer?
choices: The recurring setting can form attention while the words remain open to careful reading.
Repetition makes meaning impossible.
Translation makes the Hebrew unnecessary.
units.explanation: Liturgical repetition can deepen rather than eliminate the work of reading.

courses.subject: Halakha
courses.title: Blessings: command, community, and source chain
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on how learners trace a practice through Torah, Mishnah, Gemara, and later legal formulation—without confusing study with personal rulings.

units.hebrew: ואכלת ושבעת וברכת את ה׳ אלהיך
units.translation: You shall eat, be satisfied, and bless the Lord your God.
units.prompt: What sequence does the verse itself name?
choices: Eat, be satisfied, and bless.
Bless, then decide whether to eat.
A court procedure.
units.explanation: The verse supplies a source and sequence that later readers will receive and specify.

units.translation: Three who ate together are obligated to join in an invitation to bless.
units.prompt: What new dimension does the Mishnah bring into view?
choices: A communal form and threshold for a meal practice.
A replacement for the Torah source.
A philosophical definition of freedom.
units.explanation: A Mishnah can specify how a source enters shared practice.

units.hebrew: כל הנהנה מן העולם הזה בלא ברכה
units.translation: Whoever benefits from this world without a blessing…
units.prompt: What reading question belongs when the Gemara intensifies a practice?
choices: What claim or reason is the source adding to the practice?
Which word is easiest to memorize?
Why no context is needed.
units.explanation: Gemara reading asks what argumentative or conceptual work a statement performs.

units.translation: Source · reasoning · ruling.
units.prompt: What should a learner retain at the end of a source chain?
choices: Study traces sources and reasoning; personal application can require qualified guidance.
One brief lesson issues a ruling for every situation.
Later sources make earlier ones irrelevant.
units.explanation: The goal is literate, responsible study rather than simulated authority.

courses.subject: Torah & Tanakh
courses.title: Covenant: command, memory, and responsibility
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on close biblical reading: how command, memory, and responsibility accumulate across Torah.

units.hebrew: ואהבת את ה׳ אלהיך בכל לבבך
units.translation: Love the Lord your God with all your heart.
units.prompt: What is the first close-reading task?
choices: Identify the command and ask how the verse describes its scope.
Assume later readers erase the verse.
Treat love as source-free sentiment.
units.explanation: Begin with the source's own command and language before expanding interpretation.

units.hebrew: ואהבתם את הגר כי גרים הייתם בארץ מצרים
units.translation: Love the stranger, for you were strangers in Egypt.
units.prompt: What reason does this verse place beside its command?
choices: Collective memory of being strangers.
A ritual measurement.
A later court decision.
units.explanation: The stated reason helps reveal the moral logic of the command.

units.hebrew: וגר לא תלחץ ואתם ידעתם את נפש הגר
units.translation: You shall not oppress the stranger; you know the life of the stranger.
units.prompt: How does this source deepen the earlier command?
choices: It repeats the theme while giving another formulation of memory and responsibility.
It changes the subject to property law.
It makes context unnecessary.
units.explanation: Comparing related verses means naming both their shared concern and their distinct wording.

units.translation: Source · context · reception.
units.prompt: What should a learner preserve when later texts cite covenant language?
choices: Both the verse's own setting and the later question it is made to address.
Only the later use.
Only a loose paraphrase.
units.explanation: Reception is layered reading, not replacement.

courses.subject: Jewish Thought
courses.title: Freedom: command, agency, and argument
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on turning a familiar theme into a precise conceptual inquiry.

units.translation: Choose life.
units.prompt: What question does this imperative open?
choices: How command, agency, and responsibility relate.
Which object belongs to two claimants.
Why concepts need no definition.
units.explanation: A conceptual source begins with the question its language makes possible.

units.hebrew: כי קרוב אליך הדבר מאד בפיך ובלבבך לעשותו
units.translation: The matter is very near to you, in your mouth and heart to do it.
units.prompt: Which claim is best grounded in this verse?
choices: The verse links action to speech and inward life.
Freedom means doing whatever one wants.
The verse has no relation to action.
units.explanation: A claim should be specific enough to test against the source.

units.translation: Everything is foreseen, yet permission is given.
units.prompt: What does this compact teaching require from a careful reader?
choices: Hold two claims in tension before rushing to dissolve either one.
Ignore one half of the statement.
Treat tension as a mistake.
units.explanation: Thought often begins by identifying the exact claims a source holds together.

units.translation: Concept · claim · reason.
units.prompt: What would show real conceptual progress?
choices: Defining agency and explaining how a source supports a claim about it.
Repeating the word freedom without an argument.
Choosing a conclusion before reading.
units.explanation: A concept becomes learning when it is joined to source-grounded reasoning.

courses.subject: Mussar & Chassidus
courses.title: Responsibility: trait, courage, and practice
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on moral formation without slogans or self-punishment.

units.hebrew: במקום שאין אנשים השתדל להיות איש
units.translation: Where there are no people acting humanely, strive to be a person.
units.prompt: What trait-question does this teaching open?
choices: How a person takes responsibility when others do not.
How to avoid community forever.
How to calculate a measurement.
units.explanation: Name the trait and situation before turning a source into a practice.

units.translation: The shy person does not learn.
units.prompt: What tension does the line make visible?
choices: Humility can coexist with the courage to ask and learn.
Humility means permanent silence.
Character is unrelated to study.
units.explanation: Mussar often refines a trait by showing what it is not.

units.translation: Serve the Lord with joy.
units.prompt: How can inner posture relate to practice?
choices: It can deepen action without replacing its concrete form.
Feeling alone makes action irrelevant.
Practice makes intention irrelevant.
units.explanation: The aim is integration of inner life and action.

units.translation: Source · trait · small practice.
units.prompt: What is a responsible next step after study?
choices: Choose a modest practice to revisit, rather than making a sweeping self-judgment.
Promise never to struggle again.
Forget the source entirely.
units.explanation: Formation is specific, repeatable, and anchored in a source.

courses.subject: Jewish History
courses.title: Rabbinic worlds: place, institution, and memory
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on placing Jewish texts in communities without reducing them to background.

units.translation: Land of Israel · Babylonia.
units.prompt: What question does this pair make possible?
choices: How location, language, and institutions shape the questions communities face.
Why geography never matters.
Why every community is identical.
units.explanation: Place is evidence for reading, not mere decoration.

units.translation: Study house · court · community.
units.prompt: What can institutions help a learner study?
choices: How learning, law, and belonging take social form.
Why ideas have no communities.
Why dates are the only historical evidence.
units.explanation: Texts and institutions shape one another across time.

units.translation: Memory · testimony.
units.prompt: What distinction protects careful historical reading?
choices: A source can be evidence about an event and about how it was remembered.
Every source is a neutral camera.
Memory has no historical value.
units.explanation: Sources are both windows and voices.

units.translation: This is in one case; that is in another.
units.prompt: How can this reasoning move assist history?
choices: It can show that apparently conflicting accounts describe different settings.
It proves one account false without reading it.
It ends comparison immediately.
units.explanation: A reasoning habit can transfer across subjects when used with care.

courses.subject: Judaism & the Wider World
courses.title: Translation: language, exchange, and difference
courses.intro: A four-source anchor unit on comparing traditions and intellectual worlds without flattening either one.

units.translation: Language · translation · interpretation.
units.prompt: What changes when a text crosses languages?
choices: Its terms can acquire new possibilities and constraints for readers.
Meaning becomes automatic.
Original language becomes irrelevant.
units.explanation: Translation is both a linguistic and historical event.

units.translation: Question · context · similarity · difference.
units.prompt: What must a responsible comparison name?
choices: A shared question and the distinct contexts and differences of each source.
Only a shared word.
A stereotype about one tradition.
units.explanation: Comparison is disciplined close reading, not equivalence.

units.translation: Community · institution · book.
units.prompt: What historical question belongs here?
choices: Which communities and institutions made particular reading and translation possible.
Why books have no audiences.
Why social setting never affects learning.
units.explanation: Ideas move through communities, languages, and institutions.

units.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
units.prompt: What is the careful next question for wider-world study?
choices: How Jewish sources frame communal responsibility in particular historical societies.
Which verse settles every civic disagreement.
Why law and history never meet.
units.explanation: Jewish law and thought meet the wider world through concrete sources and settings.
